newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean metal industry yet unaffected by strikes.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean metal industry yet unaffected by strikes.

text.p: South Korea's metals makers have not yet been affected by the nationwide wave of strikes, and their unions are unlikely to join the stoppages for the time being, company and union officials said on Tuesday.
But company officials said they were worried their operations could be affected if strikes at such sectors as transport, carmaking and shipbuilding continued further.
Strikes have crippled much of South Korean industry after a controversial labour law was railroaded through parliament on December 26.
"Our workers are unlikely to start striking, although I can not rule out the possibility," said Lee Won-kil, a manager of Aluminium of Korea Ltd.

The company, a unit of the Hyundai Group, is South Korea's largest aluminium sheet and coil maker. Other company officials said its workers sympathised with management efforts to recover from losses over the past three years.
Officials at LG Metals Corp, LG Cable and Machinery Ltd, Korea Zinc Co and Taihan Electric Wire Co also said it was unlikely their workers would strike.
Union officials at these companies said they had no immediate plans to go on strike, although they agreed with the stance by the nation's two union umbrella groups.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions and the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions have called out its combined 1.7 million members on strike in protest at the new law.
"We have no strike plan for now, taking into account the serious damage the company had during last July's strike," said Nam Song-hee, chairman of Aluminium of Korea's union.
Union officials at Taihan and LG Metals said they would watch closely the progress of strikes in other industries.
On Tuesday President Kim Young-sam ruled out compromise over the controversial legislation, saying the law was needed to improve the nation's competitiveness.
Hours after Kim's comments, the head of the trade union confederation said he would bring out public sector unions to join stoppages.
The new law allows employers to lay off surplus workers, hire temporary staff and replace strikers.
